question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping's entrenched authority within the Chinese Communist Party and its central institutions underpins the strong market consensus against removal before 2027. Structural factors such as the absence of formal term limits for his leadership role, combined with sustained alignment across party and military bodies, have limited visible succession pressures or factional challenges in recent periods. No major disruptions from policy shifts, health announcements, or external events have altered this positioning in the past month. Late-stage developments including sudden illness, elite-level disagreements over economic direction, or unforeseen geopolitical crises could still introduce volatility within the short resolution window.

eventMetadata.context_description: The crowded 2028 Democratic field remains wide open more than two years before primaries, with no candidate securing broad commitments or dominant polling leads. Trader consensus positions Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez narrowly ahead due to her high name recognition, large social media following, and appeal among progressive voters, while Jon Ossoff and Gavin Newsom trail closely amid buzz around their Senate and gubernatorial records. Recent DNC approval of a revised primary calendar—starting with South Carolina in January 2028—could shift early dynamics toward candidates strong with Black, Latino, and union voters. Most potential contenders have avoided formal declarations, leaving room for shifts from midterm results, policy debates, or emerging endorsements before the race consolidates.
